newsitem.title: USA: Motorola expected to report lower earnings.
newsitem.headline: Motorola expected to report lower earnings.

text.p: Motorola Inc. is expected to report lower earnings for the third consecutive quarter Thursday, but analysts will be looking for hints of a rebound in its key semiconductor and wireless phone businesses.
Motorola said it will release fourth quarter results after the market closes on Thursday.

According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates is 41 cents a share, compared with 72 cents a share for the year-earlier period. In last year's fourth quarter Motorola earned $432 million on sales of $7.3 billion.
For all of 1995, Motorola reported profits of $1.78 billion on sales of $27 billion.
"I suspect investors are going to be looking harder at new orders, particularly in the semiconductor sector," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst for Brown Brothers Harriman.
Motorola declined to comment on its earnings.
The stock of Schaumburg, Ill.-based Motorola rose $1.875 to $63.375 in late New York Stock Exchange trading after Morgan, Stanley raised its rating on the company.
While Motorola's fourth quarter earnings are expected to fall some 43 percent from a year ago, analysts said the profits were nonetheless likely to roughly match their forecasts.
Motorola's semiconductor and wireless telephone businesses dragged sales lower for the two previous quarters -- the first time since 1985 Motorola has seen sales declines.
"I'm actually looking at revenue declining 6 percent, at about $6.9 billion" for the fourth quarter, said Monish Bahl, an analyst for Parker/Hunter Inc.
Analysts said they expected to see at least an indication of a slight turnaround, especially in semiconductors, which accounted for about 29 percent of Motorola's sales in 1995.
"The semiconductor business seems to have picked up in the end of the year," Wilkes said.
Despite the optimism, analysts said Motorola's chip business was still lagging behind the industry as a whole.

The Semiconductor Industry Association said the chip industry's book-to-bill ratio, an indicator of future demand, was 1.15 in November, up from a revised 1.11 in October. The ratio measures new orders against shipments.
Last quarter Motorola had a book-to-bill ratio of 0.82, meaning it had $82 of new orders for every $100 in shipments. Bahl said he was looking for a ratio of 0.95 to 1.00 for this quarter.
"I think that semiconductors have really bottomed out," Bahl said.

In Motorola's general systems sector, which includes wireless phone handsets that have been hit by stiff competition and pricing pressure, analysts said they also expected to see at least a slight rebound. The sector accounted for about 36 percent of Motorola's sales in 1995.
"They're rolling out some new handsets and may show some improvement," Wilkes said, adding Motorola has launched a new digital phone in Europe and has two others ready for 1997.
Motorola is expected to report a one-time charge related to layoffs last quarter, mainly in the semiconductor sector. When the company reported third quarter earnings, it said to expect the charge.
But analysts said the cutbacks were helping.

Overall, some analysts said they were looking for a more notable turnaround in the second half of 1997, as changes from the new management begin to show up. Christopher Galvin was promoted to chief executive, and the former chief executive Gary Tooker serves as chairman.

"The second half looks much better... I think it's going to become a second-half story," Hambrecht & Quist analyst Rakesh Sood said, adding that the quarter ended in March tends to be seasonally slow.
"Like any large organisation, it takes a while for the changes to take hold," Sood said.
